extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; policymakers considering limits of state power
extracted.subtask_description: Articulates normative principles for when government ought or ought not to interfere with individuals, families, education, and local institutions—balancing individual liberty, third-party harms, civic development, and administrative efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: No right to alienate one's liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of freedom cannot require that he should be free not to be free. It is not freedom, to be allowed to alienate his freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selling oneself into slavery is used as the example: allowing a person to permanently alienate their future liberty defeats the justification for permitting individuals to dispose of themselves. Laws and principles of liberty should therefore prohibit irrevocable abdications of fundamental freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reliance and third-party consequences in enforcing engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person, either by express promise or by conduct, has encouraged another to rely upon his continuing to act in a certain way ... a new series of moral obligations arises on his part towards that person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations arising from induced reliance or from consequences to third parties (e.g., children born of a marriage) must be taken into account when deciding whether to enforce a contract. These considerations create moral duties that may affect legal judgments about enforcement or dissolution, even if they do not always justify legal coercion to preserve a contract at all costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on legally binding personal-service engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagements which involve personal relations or services should never be legally binding beyond a limited duration of time; marriage, in particular, should require nothing more than the declared will of either party to dissolve it (Von Humboldt's view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal relations have a different character from commercial obligations; indefinite legal bondage in matters of personal service and feeling is inappropriate. The essay notes a distinction between legal freedom (which should not be overly constrained) and moral responsibility (which remains significant).

rubrics_metrics.name: State duty to supervise exercise of power over others (family protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The State, while it respects the liberty of each in what specially regards himself, is bound to maintain a vigilant control over his exercise of any power which it allows him to possess over others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is applied to family relations: husbands' near-despotic power over wives and parents' absolute control over children should be curtailed and equal legal protection provided. The State must protect those subject to others' power even when that power is exercised under private pretences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory universal education up to a minimum standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should require and compel the education, up to a certain standard, of every human being who is born its citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed mechanisms include public examinations starting at an early age, annual renewals with progressively broader subjects, fines or labour for negligent parents, and placement of neglected children into schooling at parental expense. Compulsory minimum education is justified as protecting children's interests and society's welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: State should avoid directing the content of education (limit indoctrination)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent the State from exercising, through these arrangements, an improper influence over opinion, the knowledge required for passing an examination ... should be confined to facts and positive science exclusively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examinations on religion or politics should test knowledge about what opinions exist and the grounds for them, not the truth of those opinions. The State may certify competence without coercively shaping citizens' conclusions on disputed matters; diversity of education and plurality of experiments is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer state enforcement/aid over state provision where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If the government would make up its mind to require for every child a good education, it might save itself the trouble of providing one ... the State can combine compulsory requirement with aid to those unable to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State should mandate education but can leave provision to private or voluntary institutions, supporting poorer children by paying fees or defraying expenses; only when society cannot provide institutions should the government directly run schools and universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates as evidence, not legal barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees, or other public certificates of scientific or professional acquirements, should be given to all who present themselves for examination, and stand the test; but such certificates should confer no advantage over competitors other than reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher examinations should be voluntary and certifications should not be permitted to exclude individuals from professions or confer legal privileges—certificates serve informational purposes for public opinion rather than legal gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three objections to government interference when providing help
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to government interference (when not infringing liberty) include: (1) individuals may do the thing better than government; (2) leaving tasks to individuals promotes civic education and development of faculties; (3) extending government functions dangerously increases its power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three objections operate as evaluative criteria. Examples: preference for jury trial and municipal self-government as civic training; voluntary associations fostering diversity of experiments; and the risk that expanding government roles creates a bureaucracy that absorbs talent and power, threatens independence, and stifles practical experience outside the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of decentralize power, centralize information
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest dissemination of power consistent with efficiency; but the greatest possible centralisation of information, and diffusion of it from the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize municipal administration with local officers handling local business while a central organ collects experience, diffuses information, advises, and enforces general rules only. Central bodies should be information hubs and supervisors, not micromanagers of local affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central superintendence limited to enforcing laws and sharing knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The central organ should have a right to know all that is done, and its special duty should be that of making the knowledge acquired in one place available for others; its actual power should be limited to compelling the local officers to obey the laws laid down for their guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In things not provided for by general rules, local officers should be left to their own judgment under responsibility to constituents; when central supervision finds non-execution it should appeal to tribunals or constituencies. Example: the Poor Law Board's intended role over Poor Rate administrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central intervention justified to prevent spillovers from local mismanagement
rubrics_metrics.description: No locality has a moral right to make itself by mismanagement a nest of pauperism, necessarily overflowing into other localities, and impairing the moral and physical condition of the whole labouring community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where local mismanagement produces harms that cross local boundaries or affect national interests, stronger central powers (coercion or subordinate legislation) may be right and necessary; such interventions are exceptions to general decentralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating national talent in the bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every function superadded to those already exercised by the government ... converts, more and more, the active and ambitious part of the public into hangers-on of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing the nation's best talents into permanent government service risks creating a dominant bureaucracy that resists change, monopolizes influence, and reduces the capacity of society outside the State to criticize or replace it. Institutions should therefore preserve opportunities outside government for forming practical ability and judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: State may legitimately restrict private acts that injure others (including marriage/parenthood rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws which forbid marriage unless the parties can show that they have the means of supporting a family, do not exceed the legitimate powers of the state ... to produce children, beyond a very small number, with the effect of reducing the reward of labour by their competition, is a serious offence against all who live by the remuneration of their labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When private acts (like marriage or procreation) foreseeably cause harm to others or society (e.g., poverty, overpopulation, reduction of labour rewards), the State is justified in imposing restrictions or social stigma; such measures are framed as preventing acts injurious to others rather than violating liberty.
